new_statements.quote: Vowel length and stress are not contrastive. Preliminary observations would suggest primary stress is placed on the first syllable.7 Understanding how stress placement is affected by verbal morphology, and how stress affects the length of syllables (both stressed and unstressed), requires further research. [p. 32] ... Secondly, even in the Korobāri dialect, stress-placement indicates the contrast: stress falls on the first syllable of the main verb. Therefore if the conjunctive participle suffix is being used, stress falls on the first syllable of the inflected verb (391c), whereas if the absolutive is being used, stress falls on the first syllable of the non-finite verb (391b). [p. 227]

Wilde) and extracted the pages with extracted text. PDF p.54 = book p.32, sec. 2.5 'Nasalisation, length and stress', reads exactly: 'Vowel length and stress are not contrastive. Preliminary observations would suggest primary stress is placed on the first syllable.7 Understanding how stress placement is affected by verbal morphology, and how stress affects the length of syllables (both stressed and unstressed), requires further research.' Fn. 7 (pp.32-33) quotes Klaiman 1987:499 on Bengali non-phonemic word-initial stress, as reported. PDF p.249 = book p.227, sec. 3.7.10, reads exa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word (stated as a preliminary observation); in verb forms stress sits on the first syllable of the main verb, so a stress shift diagnoses conjunctive participle vs absolutive.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; author flags interaction with verbal morphology and syllable length as needing further research. Phrase-level focus prominence is treated separately (ch. 7: focused elements attract stress and high pitch).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word; case markers 'do not carry stress'); verb-form diagnostic at p. 227 is word-internal. Data are mainly the Jhāpā dialects (Ghailāḍubbā, Lakharigaddi, Korobāri); the Morang dialects (Dādar Bairiā, Rangeli) — the area Glottolog identifies with Kayort — were studied only for the agreement system, and no stress remark is tied to them specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: Kayort [kyv] / kayo1247 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry with zero descriptive references: Glottolog 5.3 rules that the Ethnologue 'Kayort' of Morang district, eastern Nepal, is covered by Toulmin's Rangeli-Rajbanshi data and 'is to be equated with Rajbanshi [rjs]' = rajb1243, which is already in the catalog (fixed: initial syllable, Wilde 2008). ISO 639-3 still lists kyv as active; Ethnologue and Wikipedia now call it 'Kewat', and Wikipedia says no grammar, phonology or corpus exists for it. Wilde 2008's Rajbanshi data come mainly from Jhāpā, with the Morang dialects (Dādar Bairiā, Rangeli) covered only for agreement; Rangeli, Morang is exactly the site behind Glottolog's equation. No work exists under the names Kayort/Kewat.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 p.32 (PDF p.54): stress and vowel length not contrastive; preliminary observations put primary stress on the first syllable; fn.7 compares Bengali initial stress (Klaiman 1987:499). Sec. 3.7.10 p.227 (PDF p.249): 'stress falls on the first syllable of the main verb'. Data mainly Jhāpā dialects; Morang dialects (Dādar Bairiā and Rangeli) studied for the secondary agreement system (pp.5-6), informant Badri Nārāyan Rājbanshi of Rangeli; no stress remark specific to the Morang dialects.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Identity ruling: 'E16/. has an entry Kayort [kyv], a language related to Bengali in Morang district of Eastern Nepal. The Rangeli-Rajbanshi [rjs] data from Matthew Toulmin 2006 covers this area (cf. George van Driem 2001: 1146) and there is no other Bengali related lect spoken there.. Thus the Kayort [kyv] entry is to be equated with Rajbanshi [rjs].' Zero descriptive references.
